title: THEY ENTERED WITH GREAT POMP—BUT THE PRISONER WAS THE FREEST MAN IN THE ROOM
paragraphs: THEY ENTERED WITH GREAT POMP—BUT THE PRISONER WAS THE FREEST MAN IN THE ROOM

Agrippa and Bernice walked into Paul’s hearing surrounded by power, prestige, commanders, and the prominent people of Caesarea. Paul walked in wearing chains. Yet before the hearing was over, the man who appeared to have nothing would speak about the one treasure no throne could give: Jesus Christ.
There must have been a moment when everyone looked toward the entrance.
You can almost hear the room changing.
Footsteps.
Movement.
Whispers.
Then royalty appeared.
Acts 25:23 describes the entrance of King Agrippa and Bernice with a phrase so vivid that Luke seems determined for us not to miss the spectacle:
“μετὰ πολλῆς φαντασίας” — meta pollēs phantasias.
“With great pomp.”

The Greek word φαντασία (phantasia) carries the idea of outward display, show, splendor, or impressive appearance. This is not the modern psychological meaning of “fantasy.” Luke is describing a conspicuous public spectacle.
And it was quite a spectacle.
Agrippa and Bernice entered the audience hall accompanied by military commanders and the prominent men of Caesarea.
Imagine the contrast.
Authority walked in.
Wealth walked in.
Reputation walked in.
Military rank walked in.
Social importance walked in.
Then Festus gave the command...
and Paul was brought in.
A prisoner.
No royal procession.
No impressive entourage.
No earthly throne.
No expensive display Luke considered worth mentioning.
Just a man whose freedom had been taken from him.
And chains.
But appearances were about to become dangerously misleading.
Because sometimes the person everybody envies is imprisoned by things nobody can see.
And sometimes the person everybody pities possesses a freedom nobody in the room understands.
That is what makes this scene so haunting.
Agrippa looked powerful.
Paul looked powerless.
Agrippa could sit in honor.
Paul had to stand accused.
Agrippa possessed political status.
Paul possessed something Rome could neither manufacture nor confiscate.
He knew the risen Jesus.
And suddenly Acts 25 is no longer merely an ancient courtroom scene.
It becomes a mirror.
Because we still live in a world of φαντασία.
Great display.
We have simply changed the costumes.
We have carefully selected photographs.
Titles.
Followers.
Achievements.
Cars.
Houses.
Clothes.
Platforms.
Careers.
Ministries.
Perfect-looking marriages.
Perfect-looking families.
Even perfect-looking Christianity.
We have learned how to walk into rooms with our own version of “great pomp” while hiding wounds nobody is allowed to touch.
Some people know exactly how to appear blessed while quietly falling apart.
Some know how to worship publicly while wrestling with secret sin privately.
Some can quote Scripture while carrying bitterness they refuse to surrender.
Some can encourage everyone else while wondering whether God still hears them.
Some have become masters at looking spiritually alive.
And Jesus still sees behind the procession.
He sees what applause cannot heal.
He sees what money cannot forgive.
He sees what religious performance cannot cleanse.
He sees the person beneath the image.
That is why Paul's appearance before Agrippa matters so much.
The story does not end with Acts 25:23.
The pomp is only the entrance.
The real confrontation happens when the prisoner begins speaking.
Paul stretches out his hand and tells his story.
He speaks about his former life.
His religious zeal.
His opposition to Jesus.
His persecution of Christians.
He does not polish his past until it becomes respectable.
Paul had participated in something terrible.

He says that he imprisoned many of the saints and, when they were put to death, cast his vote against them. He says he punished believers repeatedly in the synagogues and tried to force them to blaspheme. In his rage against them, he pursued them even into foreign cities.
This is Paul before grace.
Not merely confused.
Not merely imperfect.
He was violently opposed to the people of Jesus.
And then came the road.
Damascus.
Midday.
A light from heaven brighter than the sun.
Everyone fell to the ground.
Then Paul heard a voice.

Acts 26:14 preserves something remarkable: Paul says the voice spoke to him “τῇ Ἑβραΐδι διαλέκτῳ”—in the Hebrew language or Hebrew dialect, a wording commonly understood in this setting to refer to the Jewish Semitic language Paul spoke, often identified as Aramaic.
And the voice said:
“Σαούλ, Σαούλ, τί με διώκεις;”
Saoul, Saoul, ti me diōkeis?
“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?”
Then Paul asked:
“Who are You, Lord?”
And came the answer that shattered his world:
“Ἐγώ εἰμι Ἰησοῦς ὃν σὺ διώκεις.”
Egō eimi Iēsous hon sy diōkeis.
“I am Jesus whom you are persecuting.”
Jesus.
The One Saul believed he was opposing in the name of God was speaking to him from glory.
Think about that moment.
Paul had been wrong about Jesus.
Terribly wrong.
Yet Christ did not destroy him on the Damascus road.
He confronted him.
Stopped him.
Exposed him.
And then transformed him.
That is scandal becoming grace.
The persecutor would become the preacher.
The man who dragged Christians away would eventually be dragged before rulers because he belonged to Christ.
The man who once tried to silence testimony about Jesus would spend the rest of his life giving testimony about Jesus.
The enemy became an ambassador.
Not because Paul's past suddenly became innocent.
Grace does not rewrite history by pretending sin never happened.
Grace rewrites the sinner.
That distinction matters.
Christianity does not teach that sin is insignificant.
It teaches something infinitely more astonishing:
Sin is so serious that Christ went to the cross...
and grace is so powerful that the sinner who comes to Christ does not have to remain who he was.
Paul would later write:
Ei tis en Christō, kainē ktisis.
“If anyone is in Christ, [there is] a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17).
Not improved decoration over the old ruins.
New creation.
That is the Gospel.
And perhaps this is where Paul's hearing stops feeling ancient.
Because maybe you know what it means to carry a past.
Maybe there are chapters of your life you desperately wish you could tear out.
Things you did.
Things you said.
People you hurt.
Promises you broke.
Years you wasted.
Secret habits.
Private compromises.
Perhaps everybody sees your “great pomp” while you remember what happened when nobody was watching.
Maybe you have even wondered:
“If people really knew me, would they still love me?”
And beneath that question is an even deeper one:
“If God really knows me, could He possibly still want me?”
Paul's life answers that question without making sin small.
Jesus knew exactly who Saul was when He stopped him.
Christ did not discover Paul's history afterward.
There was no surprise in heaven.
Jesus confronted Saul while Saul was still the persecutor.
And grace met him there.
But grace did not leave him there.
That is something our generation desperately needs to recover.
Jesus does not merely offer affirmation.
He offers resurrection.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He changes allegiance.
He changes direction.
He gives new life.
The Gospel is not Jesus helping you become a more comfortable version of yourself.
It is reconciliation with God through the crucified and risen Christ.
Paul understood that.
So standing before Agrippa, Paul does something extraordinary.
He does not merely defend himself.
He preaches.
Imagine the reversal.
Paul is technically the prisoner.
Yet Paul begins speaking as though something infinitely greater than his legal survival is at stake.
Because it is.
A soul is listening.

Paul tells Agrippa that his message is consistent with what Moses and the prophets said would happen: that the Christ would suffer and, by rising from the dead, proclaim light to both the Jewish people and the Gentiles.
Festus interrupts him.
“Paul, you are out of your mind!”
But Paul does not retaliate.
He answers respectfully:
“I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words.”
Then he turns toward the king.
And everything becomes personal.
“King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.”
What a moment.
The prisoner is asking the king the question.
The accused man is speaking to the conscience of the ruler.
Paul could have spent every breath begging for freedom.
Instead, his heart reaches toward Agrippa.
Then Agrippa responds with the famous line translated in different ways because the Greek is terse and its precise nuance has been debated:
“Ἐν ὀλίγῳ με πείθεις Χριστιανὸν ποιῆσαι.”
En oligō me peitheis Christianon poiēsai.

Translations vary. It has traditionally been rendered along the lines of, “Almost you persuade me to become a Christian,” while many modern translations understand Agrippa as asking whether Paul thinks he can persuade him to become a Christian “in such a short time.”
We should not build theology on a certainty the Greek itself does not give us.
But Paul's answer is unmistakable.
“Whether in a short or long time, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am—except for these chains.”
Read that slowly.
Except for these chains.
Paul wanted them to have what he had.
The prisoner wanted the king to become like him.
Now we understand who possessed the greater treasure in that room.
Paul had chains around his body.
But Christ had freed his soul.
Agrippa had status.
Paul had Christ.
Bernice had spectacle.
Paul had testimony.
Festus had governmental authority.
Paul had a commission from heaven.
The prominent men of Caesarea had reputation.
Paul had redemption.
And when death eventually came for every person in that room, the pomp could not follow any of them into eternity.
Neither can ours.
Your followers cannot save you.
Your bank account cannot reconcile you to God.
Your achievements cannot remove guilt.
Your religious reputation cannot substitute for repentance.
Your church attendance cannot become your Savior.
Your family name cannot become your righteousness.
Your good deeds cannot turn Calvary into something unnecessary.
You need Jesus.
Not Christianity as decoration.
Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Lord.
King.
Savior.
And perhaps the most dangerous place spiritually is not open rebellion.
Perhaps it is being almost persuaded.
Close enough to hear.
Close enough to feel conviction.
Close enough to know something must change.
But always postponing surrender.
Tomorrow.
Later.
When life settles down.
When the addiction is under control.
When you have enjoyed yourself a little longer.
When you understand everything.
When you feel worthy.
But nobody becomes worthy enough to need less grace.
Paul himself was living evidence.
The Gospel is not the announcement that worthy people may approach Jesus.
It is the announcement that Christ died for sinners.
That means you can stop hiding.
You can stop rehearsing your résumé before God.
You can stop pretending the wound isn't bleeding.
You can stop polishing the chains and calling them jewelry.
Bring the truth into the light.
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
The same Jesus who confronted Saul is still the Jesus whose grace can transform a human life.
Maybe your Damascus road will not include a light brighter than the sun.
Maybe there will be no audible voice.
But perhaps this moment is quieter.
A screen.
A room.
A sentence you almost scrolled past.
And suddenly something inside you knows:
I cannot keep living like this.
Then don't turn conviction into another forgotten moment.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess what you have hidden.
Ask Him for mercy.
Trust in His death and resurrection rather than your ability to repair yourself.
If you have wandered from Him, come home.
If you have been performing Christianity while secretly starving, stop performing.
If you have never surrendered your life to Christ, do not confuse being near Christian things with belonging to Jesus.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail of your life. But you can make one small act of honesty.
Someone reading the comments may need to discover that Christians are not people without scars.
We are people whose scars no longer get the final word.
And please do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Jesus Christ purchased our redemption, and salvation is God's gift of grace received through faith—not a product anyone can buy.

But if Gospel-centered work has helped you and you want to help it reach another exhausted believer, another wandering son or daughter, another person hiding behind appearances, you can support that work practically.
Sharing is one simple way.
Send this privately to the friend who looks strong but has not sounded like themselves lately.
Not to prove that you glorify God.
Not to purchase spiritual favor.
But as a voluntary way of supporting work you believe helps glorify God by proclaiming Christ.
Use them.
Read.
Study Scripture.
Test what you read against God's Word.
Grow.
Then help someone else grow.
Because someday every procession ends.
Every title is surrendered.
Every audience goes home.
Every spotlight goes dark.
Every possession changes hands.
Agrippa's pomp disappeared centuries ago.
But the testimony spoken by a chained apostle in that room is still traveling across the earth.
And perhaps tonight it traveled all the way to you.
That may be the deepest irony of Acts 25 and 26.
The room was filled with important people.
Yet history remembers the prisoner.
Not because Paul made himself great.
Because Paul belonged to Jesus.
So when your past tells you that your story is already ruined, remember Saul.
When shame tells you that God could never use someone like you, remember Damascus.
When appearances convince you that everyone else is doing better than you, remember Agrippa's entrance.
When obedience costs you something, remember Paul's chains.
When you are tempted to trade faithfulness for applause, remember that pomp has an expiration date.
And when you wonder whether Jesus can do anything meaningful with the wreckage you handed Him...
look at the persecutor who became an apostle.
Look at the prisoner who preached to kings.
Look at the sinner who discovered grace.
Then look toward the cross.
Because the center of this story was never Paul.
It was always Jesus.
Jesus confronted him.
Jesus forgave him.
Jesus commissioned him.
Jesus sustained him.
Jesus became the reason chains could not silence him.
And Jesus is still the only One who can take a story marked by sin, shame, failure, pride, hypocrisy, addiction, bitterness, regret, and brokenness—and redeem the person inside it.
So share this if someone needs that reminder.
But above everything else—
follow Jesus.
Because you can lose the applause and still have Christ.
You can lose the title and still have Christ.
You can lose the room and still have Christ.
You can even wear chains...
and still be the freest person there.
The world may remember the spectacle for a moment, but eternity remembers what we did with Jesus.
